The Salt card, a credit card-sized device, aims to simplify smartphone and tablet unlocking by automatically doing so when the user is within 10 feet (three meters). It connects via Bluetooth and sends notifications if the user strays too far from their wallet. The founders claim it saves around 53 hours over a year based on the average phone unlocking 150 times daily. The card, made of durable plastic, has a battery life of 18 months. The creators claim it is more secure than fingerprint scanners and workable with gloves in winter. The Salt card starts at $20 and is currently available for purchase. It is also hoped to develop the device as a platform for communicating with various electronic devices.

1. Middlesbrough's Patrick Bamford scored two goals to lead his team to a crucial victory over Wolves, keeping them in contention for promotion to the Premier League.
2. Bamford, currently on loan from Chelsea, has been instrumental in Boro's success, and manager Aitor Karanka believes he could be a key player if they secure promotion.
3. With three matches left in the Championship season, Middlesbrough must win all of them to have a chance at automatic promotion, starting with a trip to Norwich on Friday.

The article focuses on the trial of Oskar Groening, known as the 'Auschwitz bookkeeper,' while highlighting the forgotten roles of women who served as guards at Nazi death camps, such as Ravensbrück and Auschwitz. Seven decades later, only three of the 3,700 women who served as guards have been investigated by German prosecutors for their roles as accomplices to mass murder. The women, including Charlotte S, a former Ravensbrück and Auschwitz guard, and Gisela S, a harsh disciplinarian at Auschwitz, are deemed too ill or infirm to face trial. Meanwhile, Oskar Groening, a former SS sergeant, is being charged with 300,000 counts of accessory to murder. An ongoing debate exists about whether it is too late for justice in these cases, with historians viewing the slow pace of investigations and trials as a failure to hold those responsible accountable.

Alastair Cook and Jonathan Trott struggled with the bat in the first Test against West Indies, with both players dismissed cheaply. Cook failed twice in the first Test, while Trott scored just four runs in his first innings and a duck in the second. James Tredwell was England's standout bowler, picking up four wickets in the match, but England still struggled to gain a significant advantage, ending the second innings with a lead of 220. Jermaine Blackwood was the star for West Indies, scoring a maiden Test century in his sixth match.

A technological innovation in Israel claims to transform any smartphone into a Star Trek-style tricorder, capable of identifying chemical components of various objects from a distance. The system, developed by Unispectral Technologies and Tel Aviv University, uses hyperspectral imaging to analyze a material's unique chemical fingerprint, and has already patented the optical part of the system. The team anticipates wide-ranging applications in industries such as healthcare, food and drink, and the defense sector. The technology is currently under discussion for integration with major smartphone makers, automotive companies, and wearable device manufacturers. This advancement follows other efforts to recreate the Tricorder, such as the Scanadu Scout and ScanNurse, which aim to revolutionize healthcare diagnostics and monitoring.

Police are searching for Peter Fox, 26, accused of murdering his mother Bernadette Fox, 57, and sister Sarah Fox, 27, in Bootle, Merseyside. The victims were found half a mile apart, with Sarah's body discovered on Thursday evening and Bernadette's body found later at sheltered accommodation. Detectives have released CCTV footage showing Peter leaving Liverpool Lime Street at 8.18pm on Wednesday and arriving at Euston railway station in London at 10.57pm. The family is urging Peter to come forward and is appealing for public help in finding him. The motive behind the murders remains unclear.

The Boston Athletic Association is opening a new facility called Boston RunBase on April 16, which will serve as a combination clubhouse, interactive museum, and retail store. This will give the association a year-round, public presence and allow visitors to learn about the Boston Marathon, run a replica course on a treadmill, or see artifacts from its 118-year history. The location is significant as it is just a few blocks from the marathon finish line and near the site of the 2013 bombing. The Boston RunBase will be a shoeseum of sorts that offers a unique Boston Marathon experience, with special events, clinics, and meet-ups for recreational joggers, lockers, showers, and a connection to the marathon's rich history.

Sarah Vine, a writer and columnist, expresses her interest in taking Jeremy Clarkson's job on Top Gear, arguing that the love of cars is not gender-specific. She describes her life-long affection for cars, from her childhood memories of falling asleep in her parents' Mini Cooper to her various car ownership experiences. Vine suggests that cars represent freedom, possibility, and adventure, and she is not a car snob. Despite facing criticism and abuse towards women in the car industry, Vine argues that she is a capable driver and enjoys the control and intellectual challenge of driving. She believes that being in control behind the wheel brings her joy and satisfaction.

The article highlights new research suggesting that advanced paternal age (over 35) could increase the risk of various health problems in offspring, including epilepsy, autism, breast cancer, and genetic disorders. This is because the quality of sperm declines with age, leading to DNA mutations and defects. Older fathers may also experience lower testosterone levels and poorer semen quality. The researchers recommend that would-be fathers be better informed about these risks, and that the medical community begins to educate couples on the male biological clock in the same way they do for women. The article concludes that current counseling for couples often only focuses on maternal age and quality, but does not address the potential risks associated with advanced paternal age.

1. A video has been released by Florida's Bay County Sheriff's Department showing hundreds of spring breakers on a beach in Panama City Beach, Florida, not intervening as a 19-year-old unconscious girl was gang raped by a group of men in plain sight.

2. Two suspects, Delonte Martistee, 22, of Bainbridge, Georgia, and Ryan Calhoun, 23, of Mobile, Alabama, have been arrested and charged with sexual battery for the incident, which is believed to have occurred between March 10 and 12.

3. Bay County Sheriff Frank McKeithen described the video as the "most disgusting, sickening thing" he had ever seen and criticized the bystanders for their lack of action, stating that they were more concerned about spilling their beer than someone being raped.

A mother, Kate Roberts, successfully raised £2,000 in 24 hours to pay for a specialized helmet for her son Miles, who was born with flat-head syndrome (brachycephaly). Despite being told by doctors that the condition is cosmetic and not medically dangerous, thus not covered by the NHS, the mother was concerned about the potential long-term effects, such as facial disfigurement and sight loss. After researching online, she discovered a private clinic that recommended helmet therapy, which applies pressure to the bulging parts of the baby's skull and relieves pressure from the flatter parts. The treatment costs around £2,000, which was collected through a GoFundMe campaign and local fundraising efforts.

1. A new review suggests that movements and acting out dreams during rapid eye movement sleep (RBD) could be an early sign of Parkinson's disease, as up to 90% of people with RBD may develop a neurological condition within a decade, including Parkinson's.

2. RBD is characterized by vivid dreams that the person acts out physically during sleep, ranging from hand movements to thrashing around, punching, kicking, and even jumping out of bed.

3. RBD is treatable with high doses of sleep hormone melatonin and low doses of the anti-anxiety drug clonazepam, and while it is not curable, it can be managed. The condition could potentially serve as a useful warning sign for Parkinson's disease.

The article discusses Raheem Sterling's decision not to sign a new contract at Liverpool, as stated in a recent interview. The decision has received negative reactions from Liverpool fans, who view it as ill-timed and lacking in appreciation for the club that nurtured him. Some fans are now advocating for Sterling to leave, with Liverpool potentially negotiating a move to Arsenal. Despite Sterling's potential and raw abilities, many believe his development would be better served at Liverpool under manager Brendan Rodgers. This situation has been a source of frustration among fans, who maintain that no player is bigger than the club.

Daryl Clark, Man of Steel and current Warrington Wolves player, will face his former team Castleford Tigers, his boyhood club, in a Super League match on Easter Monday. Clark was persuaded by Warrington coach Tony Smith to leave Castleford and has maintained his ever-present record for the Wolves. Castleford have had mixed results since Clark's departure, and the reception for him is expected to be positive. Meanwhile, Warrington and Castleford have a history of five consecutive home wins for Warrington, but Castleford has dropped to seventh place following a three-game losing streak. Warrington coach Tony Smith expects a positive reception for Clark from the visiting fans, praising his contributions to Castleford.

David Moore, 25, was convicted for acts of road rage after a confrontation with Rafal Cegielka, 45, who was picking up his child. He punched Mr. Cegielka through an open car window and later damaged his car with a hockey stick, causing £500 worth of damage. Moore later stated he had a 'bad day' and was angry. He was sentenced to 16 weeks in prison, suspended for two years, ordered to attend the Resolve program for violence management, and was ordered to pay £650 in compensation.

Eritrean Christian migrants have spoken of escaping death threats from Islamic State fanatics in Libya, where they were forced to deny their faith or face beheading or throat-slitting. Haben, 19, said friends were shot dead by armed ISIS terrorists patrolling the chaotic North African state. Tens of thousands are fleeing Libya due to ISIS establishments and the risk of capture and execution. The journey across the Mediterranean is perilous, with around 900 people dying in a recent boat capsizing, one of the worst maritime disasters since World War Two.

The article discusses new radar images from Europe's Sentinel-1a satellite revealing the aftermath of the Nepal earthquake in incredible detail. These images have been transformed into an interferogram, which shows a large deformation pattern of 3.2ft (1 metre) from the ground around Kathmandu. Notably, scientists discovered that Mount Everest shrank by about one inch due to the earthquake. However, it still stands at its original height of 29,029 feet, according to The Weather Channel. Furthermore, an area roughly 75 miles by 30 miles has uplifted around Kathmandu.

Sebastian Thrun, the founder of Google X laboratory, predicted that computers might soon be able to transmit human personalities, suggesting the possibility of outsourcing individual experiences and personalities into a computer. He also speculated about future inventions such as flying cars, implantable computers, and medical treatments to significantly decrease unnatural deaths. Jaron Lanier, a virtual reality pioneer, questioned the feasibility of sharing personalities and warned about the risks of technology progress, including worsening inequality and selectively tallying technological victories. Google has already patented a system for robots to download personalities online, including replicating the robot's owner, a deceased loved one, or a celebrity. The system allows for customization and transferability of the robot's personality.

The article discusses the violent urban riot in Baltimore following the burial of Freddie Gray, who died from spinal injuries after being arrested. The family and allies had asked for no protests or violence on the day of the burial but were met with chaos, including looting, arson, and clashes with police. A small group of peace activists, including clergy and residents, tried to intervene, but the riot quickly gained momentum, overshadowing the message of peaceful protest. The ripples of the violence extended to gangs in the area, including Crips and Bloods, who condemned the actions and joined forces with community leaders and the family for a press conference. Overall, the riots were met with disappointment and anger from the Gray family and their legal team, who had hoped for justice, not further violence.

A new video on social media showcases a militia of female jihadis training with machine guns in Syria, believed to be linked to the Islamic State. The women, fully veiled, are seen struggling with the weight and technique of their AK-47 rifles, some making basic mistakes. The video was shot at St Simeon's Church, which was once a popular pilgrimage site, now being used as a parade ground by the radical group. The females are suggestively British nationals, with at least 30 identified by the International Centre for the Study of Radicalisation. The training session involves various drills, chanting religious slogans, and individual showcases of shooting skills. However, the video also indicates a level of disinterest among some of the women, with some seeming more interested in the scenic Syria countryside.

A 21-year-old woman named Rochelle Coulson receives £18,000 a year in benefits due to her sleep apnoea-related illness, which she claims leaves her too tired to stay awake and pose a danger at work. She gained significant weight in four years due to eating through boredom and depression. Despite doctors urging her to lose weight to manage her condition, she believes she needs a state-funded support worker to help with meal planning. This situation has led to criticism from pressure group Taxpayers' Alliance, who argue that the benefit system should not become a 'comfort blanket' and people should 'get themselves in shape' to work. Her benefits are more than a nurse or newly-qualified teacher's starting wage.

At half-time in the Aviva Stadium, Bath, despite a standout performance by fly-half George Ford, trailed Leinster 15-5 due to structural weaknesses in scrums, lineouts, and breakdowns. In the second half, driven by Ford, Bath made a valiant comeback, coming within touching distance of winning, but ultimately falling short. Bath coach Mike Ford expressed pride in the team's determination and belief, believing that they could have won with more precision. Leinster, despite losing a player to concussion, managed to hang on for a narrow 18-15 victory.

Nigel Farage's UK Independence Party (Ukip) is experiencing a significant decline in support, according to a poll of key marginal seats by Lord Ashcroft. Ukip's vote has fallen in nine out of ten battleground constituencies, with more than half of the support in two seats and a third in most others. This departure from Ukip is not translating to increased support for the Conservative Party, with the Tories predicted to lose four seats to Labour but hold onto five others in these 10 marginal constituencies. The poll also suggests that Labour has strengthened its position since last year, with Labour set to gain four seats from the Tories, including Harrow East in West London. The Ukip leader, Nigel Farage, is currently in second place in his own constituency of Thanet South, with a gap of just 1% between him and the Conservative candidate Craig Mackinlay.

David Crossley, a 63-year-old musculoskeletal therapist from Birmingham, developed large kidney stones, which doctors link to his low fluid intake due to his busy lifestyle. He often worked through lunch and barely drank water during the week, overcompensating with occasional cups of tea or coffee. Last year, he experienced a constant, uncomfortable ache in his abdomen that led him to seek medical help. An ultrasound revealed two large stones in his right kidney that could not be passed naturally, requiring surgery. This incident emphasizes the importance of proper hydration to prevent kidney stones, especially in light of growing instances of this condition.

Additional information in the article explains that kidney stones form when waste products in the blood create crystals inside the kidneys, eventually building up into a solid lump. The stones often remain symptomless until they start blocking the ureter, causing intense pain, nausea, vomiting, frequent urination, or pain during urination. Other risk factors cited in the article include dehydration, low-carb diets, excessive salt intake, obesity, and eating excessive amounts of oxalate. Avoiding

1. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) chief Michele Leonhart is expected to resign due to allegations that DEA agents divulged sensitive information at sex parties with prostitutes, possibly arranged by Colombian drug lords.
2. A U.S. congressional committee, the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, will investigate these claims, examining the bureaucratic culture and leadership within the DEA and other Justice Department investigative agencies.
3. Leonhart's anticipated departure comes after she testified before the committee last week, admitting that while there is no evidence of information leakage, it's possible that sensitive information had been compromised. The White House, however, has declined to give Leonhart a vote of confidence.

A large, partly-molten secondary magma chamber has been discovered beneath Yellowstone National Park's supervolcano, which is the primary source of its daily carbon dioxide emissions. The new chamber, located 12 to 28 miles (19 to 45km) beneath the surface, is estimated to be 11,035 cubic miles (46,000 cubic km) in volume, approximately 4.5 times larger than the previously known smaller magma chamber. The magma in this new chamber is mainly hot rock, with only 2% being molten rock that doesn't directly pose a risk for an eruption. Prior to this discovery, researchers believed the smaller chamber, located directly beneath the surface, was responsible for the supervolcano's past eruptions 2 million, 1.2 million, and 640,000 years ago.

A 10-year-old boy named L.T. is accused of beating a 6-year-old boy, Lee Allan Bonneau, to death with a rock and stick on a reservation in Saskatchewan, Canada in August 2013. Initially, L.T. claimed that he had witnessed the murder committed by a stranger, but later confessed to investigators that he was the one who killed Lee. The 10-year-old has not been charged due to his young age, and the coroner's inquest is being held to determine the circumstances of the murder and make recommendations to prevent similar tragedies in the future. Lee Bonneau was temporarily in the care of his foster mother at the time of his death, and his biological mother had reportedly struggled with depression and suicidal thoughts before his death.

Chelsea Manning, convicted of espionage in 2013 for leaking classified documents, has given her first in-depth interview after announcing her intention to transition into a woman while serving her 35-year prison sentence at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. Manning, now named Chelsea Elizabeth Manning, describes the process as painful due to restrictions such as not being able to grow her hair long. She discusses her tumultuous childhood, her realization of being a woman trapped in a man's body, and her journey that led to enlisting in the military despite a difficult training period. She is currently serving her sentence, with the possibility of parole in about seven years.

Jack Wilshere, a midfielder for Arsenal, has the potential to be a key player for the club, but former player Ray Parlour expresses concerns about his injury record, comparing it to that of Abou Diaby. Wilshere was on the bench for Arsenal's FA Cup match against Reading due to a five-month injury layoff. If Wilshere can stay fit, Parlour believes he can play a significant role in the team's future success, with the right additions to the squad. Arsenal reached the FA Cup final for the second consecutive year, and Parlour thinks their current core of players, including Wilshere, Ozil, Ramsey, and Sanchez, could be ready to compete for top honors again.

A vigilante group called Wicked Pickets, angry about offensive slogans promoting violence against women on campervans operated by Wicked Campers, started painting over the slogans after the company's CEO invited people to do so. The group believes the slogans, which include phrases like "Flash your t**s at the driver" and "A wife: An attachment you screw on the bed to get the housework done," are harmful and misogynistic and contribute to violence against women. The company apologized for the offense caused, stating they are a "cash for chaos" company that supports free speech and pushing the limits of humor, but there is currently no law to enforce the removal of the slogans. The group plans to seek a meeting with the Attorney-General of Queensland to begin the process of introducing a law to ban such slogans.

1. Northampton Saints, currently in a slump and fresh off significant international duties, aim to regain their momentum in the Premiership title race against top-of-the-table rivals Saracens, who have recently shown signs of struggling.

2. England flanker Tom Wood emphasizes the importance of a strong scrum and set piece for Saints, stating that recent defeats have exposed vulnerabilities that they must address in order to reclaim their title-challenger status.

3. Northampton has been bolstered by the return of key players like England lock Courtney Lawes, while their opponents, Harlequins, are playing in their final matches for the season with Ugo Monye preparing for retirement, setting the stage for an emotional and significant showdown.

A German man named Micha Stunz, 45, has permanently enlarged his penis with silicone injections, claiming it is now 9 inches long and weighs up to 9.5lbs (4.3kg). Despite the challenges it presents in daily life and the difficulties it causes during sex, Mr. Stunz considers it a personal preference that enhances his creativity in the bedroom. He uses a satchel to cover his groin area in public and refrains from discussing his condition with certain individuals. The silicone procedure, while popular among some men due to societal pressures on penis size, carries risks such as infection and tissue damage.

A grieving mother, Kezzia French, will hold a second funeral for her six-month-old daughter Andrea, who was killed by her father in 1999. Fourteen years later, French learned that police had removed Andrea's vital organs without her consent and had her brain cremated without her knowledge. The second funeral is scheduled to take place tomorrow in Ipswich, Suffolk, as French seeks closure and the return of her daughter's entire body.

Two friends, Jamie Jewitt and Henry Rogers, shedding significant weight and achieving successful modeling careers demonstrate that determination and self-belief can lead to achieving dreams. Both men struggled with self-esteem issues in their teenage years, with Henry reaching 18 stone at his heaviest and Jamie weighing 15st before his 15th birthday. They now use their platform to address the "shame" around body image and insecurity among men, particularly focusing on the lack of male celebrity ambassadors discussing these issues. The duo plan to promote healthy male body image in a photoshoot with Attitude/Ateen coming out in June.

The Mail on Sunday has revealed that Qatar spent £17.2 billion on various deals, including legitimate trade and football-related ventures, during the lobbying process leading up to the 2010 FIFA World Cup vote. Detailed in the book "The Ugly Game," these transactions included considerable cash payments to several football officials, such as Michel Platini, Nicolas Leoz, and Worawi Makudi. FIFA is being called to re-examine the controversial 2022 World Cup decision in light of this new information.

1. British Guantanamo Bay detainee Shaker Aamer, who has been held for over 13 years without charge or trial, is expected to be released as early as June, according to US government sources.
2. Officials in Washington stated that the 48-year-old is likely to be transferred within weeks, with President Barack Obama prioritizing his release after White House talks with British Prime Minister David Cameron.
3. Campaigners, family members, and British government officials have welcomed the news and called for Aamer's quick transfer to his family in the UK, as he has been cleared for release twice before.

A 27-year-old mother, Jo Gilchrist, spent Valentine's Day in pain after contracting a staph infection due to sharing her best friend's makeup brush. The infection spread to her spine, causing her to be confined to a wheelchair for life and leaving her with no control over her bowel or bladder. Doctors are currently treating her with high-strength antibiotics and she will remain in hospital for another three months before returning home to her two-year-old son.

A terminally ill fundraiser named Simon Mitchell, who claimed to have celebrity contacts to aid a charity for terminally ill children, admitted stealing a laptop, a phone, and a TomTom satnav from Donna's Dream House in Blackpool, Lancashire, following a three-year investigation. The theft came months after Mitchell made headlines for organizing good deeds to raise funds for the charity, following his own lung cancer diagnosis. The charity leader, Len Curtis, expressed disappointment and betrayal, stating the stolen items had cost around £6,500 to replace. The court is scheduled to sentence Mitchell next month.

A Perth couple, Sharon and Nick Chalwell, have been struggling for over seven years to conceive, leading to nine failed rounds of IVF and one failed egg donor attempt. Their desperate plea for an egg donor on a Perth radio station resulted in 22-year-old Shannon Mann, a mother herself, offering to be their donor. Shannon has always wanted to be an egg donor, and after experiencing her own challenges with motherhood, including a reversed termination that resulted in her two-year-old son, Lucas, she feels compelled to help others. The trio is now going through the necessary counseling sessions before the donation process can begin.

Camilla Parker-Bowles, formerly considered the most hated woman in Britain due to her role in the Prince and Princess of Wales' divorce, has transformed her image over the past decade and is now loved by 50% of Britons. She is admired for her warmth, charm, and approachability, and has even contributed to Charles' increasing popularity. Her step-sons William and Harry, as well as the Queen, have grown to love her, and she has become an integral part of the Royal Family. Despite facing challenges in her public role, Camilla has shown resilience and has thrown herself into charitable work, particularly in regards to osteoporosis and women's rights. She has also built a strong relationship with the Queen, and is often seen alongside her mother-in-law.

Belle Gibson, a wellness influencer, admitted that her claims of having terminal brain cancer were fabricated. Psychologist Jo Lamble believes Gibson may suffer from a narcissism disorder and anti-social personality disorder, as she deceived her fans, lacks remorse, and exhibits other traits associated with these disorders. Lamble suggested that Gibson's actions may result from neglect in her childhood, leading her to seek attention and validation in dangerous ways, particularly through the use of social media.

1. The Liberal Democrats are bracing for a significant loss of at least 20 MPs in the upcoming election, with senior party sources predicting their total will be reduced to "in the thirties."
2. Despite this, Nick Clegg is continuing a targeted election strategy, focusing on approximately 10-15 marginal seats, including Eastleigh in Hampshire where the party previously won a by-election.
3. The Lib Dems aim to win the balance of power after the election, potentially forming part of another coalition government if they can secure a seat count in the 30s. They are looking to appeal to voters who seek a centrist alternative to the Labour-SNP alliance or a "right-wing" Conservative government.

A diverse jury was selected for the death penalty trial of James Holmes, the perpetrator of the 2012 Colorado theater shootings. The group of 24 includes a union plumber, a survivor of the Columbine High School massacre, a school teacher, and several individuals with personal experiences related to mental health and depression. The selection process, which began in January, was longer and more complex than usual due to the high profile of the case and the involvement of the death penalty and insanity plea. The trial is expected to start with opening statements in April.

1. Researchers have discovered the Bombardier beetle, a small insect, mimics a machine gun by creating and repeatedly firing explosive chemical sprays from its rear. This defensive mechanism, which has been caught on camera, is unique as it can aim the nozzle at the attacker and is capable of rapid-fire capabilities.

2. A team of researchers from the University of Arizona, MIT, and Cornell University have investigated the Bombardier beetle's firing apparatus in detail, solving a long-standing mystery and revealing its passive mechanism for pulse generation. This mechanism involves an expansion membrane in the reaction chamber that temporarily shuts off the flow of reactants during each discharge.

3. The findings suggest that the pulsed delivery allows the small Bombardier beetle to produce a large amount of defensive spray while maintaining precision, speed, and energy efficiency, making it one of the most remarkable defensive mechanisms documented in insects.

Researchers have found a rare pattern in both skin cells of human skin and desert fairy circles in Namibia, despite being seemingly unrelated. This pattern involves a polygon distribution that closely matches the distribution of skin cells. The discovery suggests that both systems might be fighting for space, which could be a significant clue in understanding the formation of the desert fairy circles, known for their unusual regular distribution but unexplained origin. A study, published in Ecological Complexity, compares the number of neighbors surrounding each system. Both skin cells and fairy circles have a majority of six neighbors, with similar percentages of other neighbor counts. The research opens up possibilities for future mathematical models explaining the formation of fairy circles.

A German rapper-turned-Islamic State terrorist, Denis Cuspert, also known as Abu Talha al-Amani, has released a propaganda music video threatening terrorist attacks in Europe, with a specific focus on Britain, Germany, and France. The video contains horrific footage of past ISIS atrocities and calls on sleeper cells to wage jihad and spill blood. The video followed reports of British police raising security levels ahead of World War I commemorative events next week. Cuspert, who once went by the stage name Deso Dogg, has a history of womanizing and has fathered children with multiple women. He has been added to the US list of global terrorists, with his assets frozen and future transactions prohibited. It's thought that 1,600 British residents have joined ISIS, with at least five leaving the UK for Syria and Iraq every week.

A 19-month-old girl named Rosannah Gundry from northwestern New South Wales, Australia, has a treatment-resistant seven kilogram cancerous tumor in her abdomen, which is pressing against her spine and vital organs. She was misdiagnosed with scoliosis when she was three months old, and was eventually diagnosed with stage three neuroblastoma cancer in December last year. Despite four rounds of chemotherapy, the tumor has not shrunk to an operable size, and her family is now seeking treatment in the United States due to the tumor's resistance to available treatments in Australia. Rosannah's oncologist, family, and aunt are hopeful that a solution will be found to buy more time for the toddler. A GoFundMe page has been set up to raise funds for travel to the US for treatment.

On Saturday, an avalanche hit Everest Base Camp, scattering climbers and causing panic. The harrowing incident left at least 17 people dead, with dozens injured and several missing. Higher up the mountain, hundreds of climbers were stranded, unable to descend due to dangerous conditions caused by aftershocks and unfavorable weather. Helicopter rescues were conducted, but many remain stuck, creating ongoing concern for their safety. The number of casualties, especially among foreign climbers, is still unclear.

Jack Wilshere, Mikel Arteta, and Abou Diaby have returned to action in Arsenal's Under 21 side, with Wilshere completing 90 minutes following his serious ankle injury. Wilshere performed well in the 4-1 win over Stoke City in the U21 Premier League, creating opportunities and nearly scoring a goal himself. Notably, Alex Iwobi stole the show with a hat-trick for Arsenal in the match. Despite being capped for England's youth teams, Iwobi is expected to represent Nigeria in the future. Diaby was Arsenal's most influential performer, causing problems for Stoke's defense and coming close to scoring on two occasions. The win keeps Arsenal's Under 21 team in contention for a promotion spot to the top division.

Neil Moore, on remand for a £1.8 million fraud at Wandsworth Prison, escaped by sending a fake email posing as a court clerk. The email granted him temporary bail, allowing him to walk out of the prison. Moore's escape was motivated by his fear of inmate retaliation after forming a relationship with a transgender individual in the prison. Investigation revealed that Moore set up a fake website under the Royal Courts of Justice's name, using an email address similar to the court service's. His escape was described as sophisticated and ingenious by the judge, who also pointed out the need to deter others from attempting similar escapes. Moore was subsequently jailed for seven years after admitting eight counts of fraud.

1. Doctors are warning against cutting entire food groups, particularly carbohydrates, from diets, as it can be unsustainable, damage one's relationship with food, and potentially cause harm.
2. A dietitian in Australia has highlighted the nutritional differences between white and grain bread, recommending Tip Top 9 Grain, Helga’s Lower Carb, BarleyMax Wrap, Baker’s Delight Cape Seed, and Burgen Soy Lin as healthier choices, while cautioning against highly processed varieties such as Turkish and Lebanese bread.
3. The nutritionist emphasized that while avoiding too many processed carbohydrates can be beneficial, complete elimination is not necessary, and instead, individuals should aim for healthier options.

In 13 days, Twickenham will host a rematch of the 2013 Heineken Cup Final between Toulon and Clermont Auvergne in the Champions Cup, after Toulon narrowly defeated Leinster 15-13 in extra-time with Bryan Habana scoring the decisive try. Toulon's performance was deemed unconvincing, with multiple fumbles by both sides making for a subpar contest. Despite the win, Leigh Halfpenny's composed goal-kicking and Steffon Armitage's impact as a replacement stood out for Toulon. The upcoming Toulon vs Clermont match is anticipated to be a significant event due to both teams' dominance in European rugby.

Chef Matt Kemp's anger management issues led to the collapse of his first marriage and his business, with a particularly shameful incident occurring on SBS's Heat in the Kitchen in 2004 when he verbally abused his pregnant wife. He now recognizes his past behavior and regrets it, discussing his issues on this week's episode of Insight on SBS.Former NRL player Mark Geyer also participated in the same Insight episode, sharing similar experiences with anger management issues. Both men attribute their turnarounds to their children, with Geyer crediting the pending birth of his first child as his personal turning point. Both Kemp and Geyer are urging others facing similar struggles to watch Insight and make changes in their lives.

Genetic researchers have discovered a single gene, TcSAD1, that determines the melting point of cocoa butter. This finding could lead to the creation of new types of chocolate, cosmetics, and pharmaceuticals. Additionally, plant geneticists suggest this may also lead to the development of climate-resistant cocoa plants, potentially boosting yields and farmer income. The worldwide cocoa industry, facing a projected million-tonne shortage by 2020 due to rising demand and environmental pressures, could benefit from this discovery.

1. A review conducted in Scotland has found that the death of toddler Mikaeel Kular, who was brutally killed by his mother in January 2014, could not have been predicted based on visits and assessments by social and health service workers.

2. The review noted that while Adekoya's behavior towards her son was unusual, the circumstances leading to his death were unforeseeable even though concerns were raised and he had spent time in care.

3. The review recommends 13 areas for future learning and action for various organizations, including improving support for staff, strengthening collaboration between agencies, and addressing information sharing procedures. The full report was not published due to personal information, but a summary was released.

Victoria Wasteney, a senior occupational therapist and born-again Christian, has launched an appeal after receiving a written warning for praying for a Muslim colleague and inviting her to church events. Wasteney argues that the East London NHS Foundation Trust's actions restricted her freedom of conscience and religion. The incident occurred at St John Howard Centre in Homerton, east London, where Wasteney was suspended for nine months while they investigated the complaint and later issued a written warning. Wasteney claims she was branded a "religious nutcase," and her appeal is supported by the Christian Legal Centre. The case may have implications for the right to express religious beliefs in the workplace.

Chelsea secured a significant 1-0 victory over Manchester United, with Eden Hazard's goal in the 38th minute playing a crucial role in extending their lead in the Premier League standings. Jose Mourinho's side had various players contribute to the win, including Branislav Ivanovic who dealt well with aerial threats despite Man United's dominance. Manager Mourinho was given a 7 in the player performance analysis. The struggling Radamel Falcao endured a tough day against Didier Drogba.

Three men aged 50s from the York area have been arrested on suspicion of murdering chef Claudia Lawrence, who went missing in 2009. The body of Lawrence, who was 35 at the time of her disappearance, has not been found. Police and forensic officers have been searching multiple residences in the Heworth area of York in connection with the investigation. The three arrested are understood to be linked to previous lines of inquiry. The father of Lawrence has pleaded for anyone with information to come forward. Previous arrests related to the case were made last month and last year.

A 92-year-old woman, Pamela Clothier, was admitted to the hospital, leaving her house in Battle, Sussex, empty. Upon returning, she found her possessions had been cleared out, including her beloved dog Mitzy. She criticized her son for permitting Age UK to clear out her house, believing he thought she wouldn't survive. Clothier is advocating for a change in the law to make it harder for charities to act without the homeowner's permission, and she is calling out for more protection of the elderly and their assets. Age UK, the charity involved, apologized for the ordeal and stated they had reviewed their procedures since the incident.

A fire at Paul's Hair World in Manchester's Northern Quarter led to the death of firefighter Stephen Hunt in 2013. The suspected cause was a discarded cigarette by a 15-year-old girl, who was charged with arson, but recently had the charges dropped as the judge deemed her "guilty only of being careless." Fire crews battled the extensive blaze, which partially destroyed nearby establishments. The family and colleagues of Stephen Hunt have expressed their sorrow and appreciation for his service after his death.

Sofia Vergara's attorney reaffirmed that she has no intention of destroying or using the frozen embryos she created with ex-fiance Nick Loeb, stating she is content to keep them frozen indefinitely. Loeb previously filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent Vergara from destroying them, but her legal representative deems his claims as baseless. Previously, the couple had agreed that no unilateral action could be taken concerning the embryos, and the case remains in court. It was also reported in the media that Vergara demanded her assistant act as a surrogate for their child, while Loeb allegedly sought to use the embryos himself.

The auction of 450 photos and artifacts from World War II internment camps for Japanese-Americans, including artwork created during confinement, has been canceled due to widespread opposition led by Star Trek's George Takei and the Heart Mountain Wyoming Foundation. Critics argue the works are not just art but expressions of sorrow and regret from the disenfranchised families. The items, originally collected by 'dean of American crafts' Allen Eaton, were intended for public exhibition, and Eaton himself would have opposed the sale.

A 26-year-old Australian bride-to-be, Stephanie Scott, went missing a week before her wedding, leaving her family and friends in despair. She was last seen at her workplace, Leeton High School, on Easter Sunday. Her fiancé Aaron Leeson-Woolley and police are searching for her, although her car was found 7km outside of Griffith and a 24-year-old man, Vincent Stanford, has been charged with her murder. The wedding guests, who had traveled from around the world, including Europe and the Middle East, are now tasked with making funeral arrangements instead of attending the wedding.

The Science Channel series "Chaos Caught on Camera," premiering on April 13, showcases footage captured by individuals during real-life danger and disaster situations. This includes events such as a collision between skydiving planes in Wisconsin, a tornado in Illinois, a shipwreck in the Gulf of Guinea, and a cheetah attack in Africa. The series provides raw, intense footage, followed by analysis and explanations of the incidents. Each episode aims to provide a unique perspective on the chaos, without the need for on-screen experts. The program also features extraordinary wildlife footage and survival stories.

In the future imagined by concept artist Alex Brady, a space station reminiscent of Las Vegas named 'Space Vegas' serves as a hub for extravagant entertainment and parties. Notable for its neon lights, casinos, and attractions like a Ferris wheel and a lit-up cowboy, the station also features dwellings for hundreds or thousands of people. Designs for these future space settlements include cone-shaped structures that provide artificial gravity through rotation, and reusable single-stage-to-orbit (SSTO) vehicles for travel. These illustrations, inspired by super yacht docking in Monaco and urban life on Earth, do not aim for complete accuracy but rather offer a playful, optimistic vision of space travel.

Tim Sherwood, Chris Ramsey, and Les Ferdinand forged a close friendship while working on Tottenham's youth and Under 21 programs. This bond has endured despite their current roles opposing each other in the Premier League, with Sherwood at Aston Villa and Ramsey at Queens Park Rangers (QPR), where Ferdinand works as head of football operations. Sherwood hinted that if Ramsey's tenure at QPR ends, he would seek to bring him to Villa Park, citing Ramsey's excellent coaching skills. The trio is credited for nurturing top young talents like Harry Kane, Andros Townsend, and Ryan Mason at Tottenham, also notably developing players such as Alex Pritchard and Joshua Onomah.

In the UK, popular actors often take on voiceover work for lucrative deals, despite potential conflicts with their main roles. For instance, Coronation Street actress Katy Cavanagh faced disapproval for voiceovers, including BBC iPlayer Restart, due to potential competition with the show's main rival, EastEnders. This sparked a revision in the show's ban on voiceover work, as pressure from other actors led executives to allow radio voiceovers. Some actors, like Benedict Cumberbatch and Olivia Colman, have successful voiceover careers on top of their acting work, while others, like Noel Fielding and Shane Richie, have used voiceovers to supplement their income, before achieving greater fame. Notable examples of voiceover campaigns include Liam Neeson for Tourism Ireland and Dervla Kirwan for Marks and Spencer's chocolate pudding.

Three British men, Conrad Clitheroe, Gary Cooper, and Neil Munro, were arrested in Dubai for plane spotting (writing down aircraft registration numbers) and spent two months in prisons in Dubai and Abu Dhabi. They were accused of espionage, but the charges were dropped by the Supreme Court in Abu Dhabi. The men were released, with attorney Nasser Hashem arguing that they were pursuing a passion for plane spotting and had no ill intent. This news allows Conrad Clitheroe, who suffers from a heart condition, to return home to celebrate his first wedding anniversary with his wife Valerie. The case had been a cause of concern due to Mr. Clitheroe running out of blood pressure medication while in custody. The families of the three men were helped by the charity 'Detained in Dubai' to pay for legal representation.

The article discusses the high-tech F-35 Lightning II jet, which is equipped with a $400,000 helmet that provides pilots with a 360-degree view and the ability to 'look through' the aircraft. This is achieved through six infrared cameras mounted around the plane. However, issues with the helmet's development led to significant cost overruns, and early versions had problems with turbulence, motion sickness, and green glow in night vision mode. Despite these challenges, the F-35, considered one of the most complex weapons systems ever, is estimated to cost $1.5 trillion to develop over the next 50 years. The helmet also enables pilots to share information with other nearby F-35 jets, although communication issues emerge when multiple planes are involved.

In a poll by ComRes, the Conservative Party has gained a four-point lead over Labour, with 36% of the vote compared to Labour's 32%. Millions of voters are yet to decide on their choice, making the election race the tightest since 1992. The Liberal Democrats, Ukip, and Greens trail behind with 8%, 10%, and 5% respectively. The poll indicates that the Tory lead is fragile, and both major parties are fighting to sway undecided voters. The Tories are perceived as better for economic growth, and David Cameron is favored as the preferred leader by undecided voters.

James Holmes, a former neuroscience doctoral student, is on trial for a mass shooting at a Colorado cinema in 2012, where he killed 12 people and injured 70 others after opening fire during a midnight showing of "The Dark Knight Rises." He is representing himself as insane at the time of the shootings, which prosecutors intend to contest with the death penalty. In preparation for the trial, over 9,000 potential jurors were summoned. Holmes' upbringing was described as uneventful, and he attended Westview High School, where he was known as quiet and somewhat eccentric. Holmes had been receiving psychiatric treatment from a university psychiatrist before the shooting, with concerns about his behavior being raised to a behavioral evaluation and threat assessment team, but he was not hospitalized for further evaluation.

On Saturday, Premier League leaders Chelsea host Manchester United in a crucial match for both teams. Chelsea veteran Didier Drogba scored in their last meeting, while Robin van Persie rescued a draw for United. Angel di Maria's form has been poor since October and is likely to miss out, while Juan Mata has been integral to United's rise. A United win could blow open the title race, with a trip to Arsenal on the horizon for Chelsea. Colombians Radamel Falcao and Juan Cuadrado have disappointed since their high-profile moves, and Manchester United's Wayne Rooney, who controversially chose not to join Chelsea in 2013, remains a key player for the Red Devils. The match is a chance for Jose Mourinho and Louis van Gaal to show their mettle against each other. Eden Hazard and David de Gea are the frontrunners for the PFA Player of the Year award. If Chelsea win with a significant lead, they will be considered champions in waiting.

Glenn Mason, a former NatWest bank manager, was found guilty of stealing £185,000 from his elderly customers to fund his internet gambling addiction. He has agreed to repay the entire amount from his RBS pension pot. The court heard that Mason's gambling habit began after his teenage son was injured by a roadside bomb in Afghanistan. The bank has already refunded the customers affected, and Mason's payment will serve as compensation. Julie Jeffrey and James Cato, two colleagues implicated due to Mason's attempts to cover up his crime, were sacked and charged with fraud but were later cleared after Mason's guilty plea.

The article reveals the results of a survey by Ripley's Believe It Or Not, which shows the celebrities British people would most like to have as their family members. David Beckham was voted the number one choice for a dad, followed by Ozzy Osbourne and Jonathan Ross. Holly Willoughby was voted the top choice for a mother, with Sharon Osbourne and Nicole Kidman following. Ed Sheeran and Channing Tatum were voted as the top choices for brothers, with Adele and Rhianna being popular choices for sisters. Helena Bonham Carter was chosen as the top choice as our celebrity aunt, while David Walliams was voted the person we'd most like to have as our uncle. The results suggest that British people value trust and kindness more than wealth and good looks when it comes to choosing a parental figure.

In South Africa, violent attacks against immigrants have resulted in at least five deaths and forced over 2,000 people to flee their homes. This wave of violence began in Durban two weeks ago and has since spread to Johannesburg. Immigrants, weaponized with machetes, have clashed with police, while vigilantes have targeted shops owned by immigrants. Many immigrants feel unprotected by the authorities and have started arming themselves in response. Government figures, including the President, have strongly condemned the attacks, and efforts are being made to secure the country's porous borders and address the root causes of violence, such as high unemployment and poverty rates.

Royal Dutch Shell Plc has filed a complaint in a federal court in Alaska seeking an order to remove Greenpeace activists who illegally boarded an oil drill rig, the Polar Pioneer, in the Pacific Ocean on Monday. The activists climber onto the rig's main deck and plan to unfurl a banner with the names of millions of people opposed to Arctic drilling. The activists say they will not interfere with the rig's navigation and have supplies for several days. Shell condemned the boarding and said it has met with groups against oil drilling, but does not condone the illegal tactics employed by Greenpeace.

A fashion photographer, Ian Pettigrew, is creating a series of photographs titled "Salty Girls" featuring adult women living with cystic fibrosis (CF), aiming to raise awareness about the disease and inspire those affected by it, particularly children and teens. The women pose in various stages of undress, showcasing their scars and tattooed bodies, to embrace their appearances and promote body positivity. Pettigrew believes that these images will provide hope and demonstrate a more positive future for young people with CF, as the advances in treatment are allowing more individuals to live longer.

Bruce Jenner, who won the Olympic gold in the 1980s, started a gender transition process in the mid-1980s which included hormone therapy, electrolysis, and plastic surgery to make his features more feminine. However, after meeting Kris Kardashian, he stopped the transition due to fear of publicity and shame. Jenner postponed his gender transformation dream until he could no longer keep it a secret. The two-hour ABC special tonight will publicly address his personal journey and his transition to living as a woman.

Jamelia, a Loose Women panellist, has faced criticism for suggesting that high street stores should not cater to larger sizes, specifically beyond size 20. She clarifies that she was referring to "extreme sizing" and was advocating for healthier lifestyles for young people. Her co-panellists defended her, stating they were not talking about sizes 14, 16, or 18. Despite the backlash, Jamelia stands by her comments, expressing that they were misconstrued and never intended to make people feel badly about themselves.

1. England dominated a shambolic St Kitts Invitational XI in a farcical warm-up match, with Alistair Cook making a century before retiring, and Jos Buttler, Ben Stokes, and Ian Bell contributing solid performances.
2. St Kitts, representative of a broader decline in Caribbean cricket, struggled against England's bowling, managing only 76 for 7 in a drawn match, following an initial score of 59.
3. The match highlighted concerns about the quality and purpose of warm-up matches, with England set to play 17 Tests in the next 10 months, and questions lingering over Adil Rashid and James Tredwell for the sole spinner's position in England's Test team. The performance of Gary Ballance, who struggled with form, is also a concern ahead of the first Test.

Jordan Spieth, a 21-year-old golfer, took the lead in the first round of the 79th Masters with a score of 64, making him the youngest first-round leader in Masters history. Justin Rose, aged 34, and Ernie Els, aged 45, put up a strong fight with scores of 67, but were ultimately caught up by Jason Day who matched their score in the later hours of the day. Spieth distinguished himself with six birdies in seven holes, culminating in a 25-foot birdie putt on the 18th, earning him a three-shot lead going into the second round. Rose, who has had numerous successful starts at the Masters, was also in contention, having equaled his best Masters score.

An axe-wielding robber named Shaun Andrew McKerry, known previously as "Boomerang Boy" for his history of over 1,000 offenses dating back to age 11, attempted to rob a post office store in County Durham but was subdued by the store's owner and his wife. In the incident, McKerry was identified by the shopkeeper after removing his scarf during the struggle, and CCTV footage captured McKerry's accomplice fleeing the scene. McKerry pleaded guilty to attempted robbery and has a history of numerous offenses including car chases, burglaries, witness intimidation, assaulting a police officer, and theft. His case attracted attention in the 1990s and on multiple occasions, with his mother pleading for him to be arrested, and his identity being revealed in the press after a landmark legal victory.

The article describes an incident where Ryanair steward Fernando Miguel Andrade Viseu stole a £499 Nikon camera left on a flight and listed it for sale on eBay, but the owner, teacher Aaron Galloway, noticed the listing and confronted Viseu. In an attempt to avoid being reported to the police, Viseu confessed to the theft and was subsequently arrested and charged with theft. During the arrest, police found evidence of Viseu selling 118 items on eBay, including Ray-Ban sunglasses and expensive Skullcandy headphones. Viseu pleaded guilty in court and received a six-month drug rehabilitation program, and was ordered to pay £145 costs and do 100 hours of unpaid work. Ryanair has since sacked him. Aaron, the owner of the stolen camera, expressed frustration towards Ryanair for not being able to prevent the theft and for the loss of personal photos on the camera.

Julie Creffield, a size 18 runner, was often taunted and told she was too big to run a marathon, but she completed one in 2012 and has done numerous races since. Many women believe they cannot run due to self-doubt, self-consciousness, and fear of judgment. Julie launched the ITV show's Run For Your Life campaign to encourage women to take up running, showing that anyone can find success with running and improve their physical and mental health. The campaign follows three novice runners as they train for five weeks to run 5K, and aims to motivate viewers to join them on the journey. Julie advises women to invest in a good pair of trainers, buy a supportive sports bra, team up with a friend, make steady progress, plan runs in advance, log their progress, enter races, set targets, eat well, and remember why they run to overcome self-doubt and achieve their goals. The campaign aims to show women they can run regardless of their size, shape, or ability.

Cruise ship passengers experienced a two-day ordeal at sea on the Carnival Spirit as they were trapped during Sydney's storm of the century. The ship, carrying 2,500 holidaymakers and 1,500 crew, faced huge waves as high as 40 feet, leaving many seasick and traumatized. Finally, on Wednesday, a Sydney harbour pilot boarded, and the ship safely docked at the Overseas Passenger Terminal around 10am.

Jessa Duggar, a 22-year-old star of the TLC show "19 Kids & Counting," announced she is pregnant with her first child with husband Ben Seewald, 19. The due date is November 1st, which also marks their wedding anniversary. The announcement comes after hints in late March, with pictures suggesting they could be expecting. This will be the sixth grandchild for the Duggars, and Jessa is the third child to marry, with every marriage resulting in a baby during the first year. Jessa and Ben are outspokenly pro-life, and they do not use birth control. They shared insights about their pregnancy, plans for adopting, and their honeymoon in Venice, Italy, during a special episode of "19 Kids & Counting" on Tuesday evening.

A team of students at Rice University has developed a device named Comfortably Numb to ease the pain of injections by quickly numbing the skin. The device creates a rapid chemical reaction within 60 seconds to cool the skin, and its prototype has already demonstrated a numbing effect. The device, composed of two sealed chambers containing ammonium nitrate and water, can be used for people of all ages, especially those more susceptible to pain, such as children and the elderly. The team aims to secure a provisional patent and is considering turning it into a company in the future.

The article discusses the media's tendency to refer to Hillary Clinton as "Hillary" rather than by her full name or official titles, a practice that has been more common for female candidates than male ones. This is seen as a dubious adoption of informality that reinforces gender stereotypes and may undermine Clinton's potential presidency. The article argues that presidential candidates should be addressed formally due to the gravity and importance of the position, and suggests that Clinton's use of the mononym may be strategic, aiming to make her appear more approachable while potentially reinforcing negative stereotypes about women in the workplace.

Madonna surprised Drake with an unsolicited French kiss onstage during Coachella, where she was performing. Drake's shocked and seemingly repulsed reaction was not visible to Madonna, as she kept singing and walking off. The unexpected kiss was not part of the planned routine and was described as lasting for at least three seconds. The incident sparked discussions about Madonna's intentions and Drake's comfort level with the age difference, considering that he is known to date younger women. During the performance, Madonna wore a designer shirt dress and thigh-high boots by Givenchy.

The grand National race at Aintree was won by Leighton Aspell on Many Clouds, making him the first rider since 1953 to win the race in consecutive years on different horses. Previously disillusioned with the sport, Aspell expressed gratitude for his 18-month hiatus that recharged his batteries. Many Clouds also secured victory for owner Trevor Hemmings, who had previously won the race in 2005 and 2011 with Hedgehunter and Ballabriggs, respectively. The race was a disappointment for AP McCoy, who finished fifth on Shutthefrontdoor, missing the opportunity to secure the 4,348th victory of his career and potentially saving the bookmakers up to £50 million.

1. A leaked email from Hollywood PR Peggy Siegal suggests that the Academy Awards judges did not want to give the Best Picture Award to the film "12 Years A Slave" because it was not patriotic enough towards America, with concerns about a British director portraying the US negatively.

2. The email also reveals plans for a future Hollywood adaptation of the popular British television series "Dr Who," but not for a few years.

3. The leaked emails were part of a larger data breach at Sony Pictures Entertainment in 2013, and their release by WikiLeaks has caused controversy, with Sony strongly condemning the actions of WikiLeaks.

1. Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei has demanded that all sanctions on Iran be lifted simultaneously if a nuclear deal is reached.
2. Khamenei, seeking to reassure hardline loyalists, warned about the deceptive intentions of the U.S. and accused the White House of misleading the world with its claims about the Swiss deal.
3. Khamenei remains cautious about the likelihood of a final deal by the June 30 deadline, citing concerns about potential U.S. deception in the details of the agreement.

A woman, Ranette Afonso, is set to marry Marko Conte, whom she met after he accidentally crashed into her car while she was parked, waiting for her husband to return. The fateful encounter led to a romantic connection and the pair began regularly texting shortly after the accident, which occurred in August 2013. Ranette, a lawyer, was going through a divorce at the time but found herself drifting closer to Marko. On their third date, just two months after the accident, Marko proposed and she accepted. They are planning to marry this October.

A remote Iron Age fort built by the Picts on a 20-foot-high sea stack in Scotland has been uncovered. The fort, featuring Pictish designs, appeared to have been used for extended periods and may have played a role in the Picts' naval dominance. It could potentially be a precursor to Dunnottar Castle. The site was only accessible via climbing ropes and is thought to date from the 5th to 6th century. The fort's construction materials were not local, suggesting they were imported from elsewhere in the country. Scientists hope to study the artifacts found at the site to gain more insight into the lives of the Picts who inhabited it.

A Texas A&M, Galveston professor, Irwin Horwitz, announced he would fail his entire strategic management class due to alleged cheating, disruptive behavior, and rudeness. Horwitz's emails to students and administrators detailed these issues, including personal insults, unfounded rumors, and fights among students. University officials stated that Horwitz cannot give failing grades to the entire class and each student's academic performance would be evaluated by the department head for the remainder of the semester. The university will investigate Horwitz's accusations and take disciplinary action against any students who engaged in inappropriate conduct. Horwitz indicated he would not teach the strategic management class again at the Galveston campus.

Laura Everley, 36, was diagnosed with ovarian cancer after recognizing her symptoms listed on a Facebook post. Her symptoms included bloating, back pain, constipation, and frequent urination which she initially attributed to irritable bowel syndrome and endometriosis. After a hysterectomy and biopsy, her doctors revealed the cancer had already begun to spread. She is now undergoing chemotherapy and hopes to raise awareness about the symptoms of ovarian cancer, which can be difficult to recognize in its early stages. Despite having clear cell carcinoma, a type of ovarian cancer that is usually treated with a hysterectomy, doctors are confident she can beat the disease.

A waitress named Agnese Klavina has gone missing following a night out at a celebrity club in Puerto Banus, Spain. Her disappearance is believed to be linked to Westley Capper, the son of a multi-millionaire property developer, who allegedly drove her away from the club. A blonde hair was found in the boot of the car Capper was driving, and authorities are investigating the possibility that Agnese was illegally detained, killed, and her body thrown into the sea from a motorboat belonging to Capper's family. A court in Marbella has summoned Capper and a co-accused, Craig Porter, for questioning, but both have refused to cooperate with investigators. Agnese's family and friends are currently waiting for the Spanish judge to order new DNA tests to aid the investigation.

The article discusses the sentencing of Gavin Thorman, a drugs kingpin who operated his empire from prison, HMP Altcourse. Thorman was part of a 26-member gang that conspired to supply cocaine and cannabis into North Wales. During a five-year investigation, police seized drugs worth nearly £200,000, luxury cars, guns, and a boat. Thorman, who was serving a sentence for assault, was overheard boasting about his new contacts and discussing drugs while in prison. He planned to spend his ill-gotten money on cosmetic procedures and holidays. The entire gang was caught after surveillance work by more than 200 police officers, and they were sentenced for their roles in the conspiracy, receiving a total of 127 years in prison. This sentencing was said to be the most significant in the region for one investigation.

A 21-year-old man named Chris Ball made a heartbreaking final goodbye video to his family before taking his own life, expressing love and asking them not to blame themselves. Chris was sent home from a hospital due to a shortage of beds after his mother took him there 11 days prior. Chris's mother, Kerrie Keepa, who has experienced multiple suicides in her family, is calling for more beds for suicidal youths in hospitals and emergency suicide training for hospital staff. The family is sharing the video to raise awareness about the impact of depression, which takes the lives of more young Australians than car accidents and skin cancer.

The individual claiming responsibility for the Gone Girl-like kidnapping of Denise Huskins in California has stated they will surrender upon immunity for their co-conspirators. This offer comes after the group expressed displeasure with the police labeling the incident a hoax. The kidnappers, who are linked to a series of burglaries and car thefts, allege the abduction was a training exercise, not targeted at Huskins. They have denied any intention to cause harm and claim it was a case of mistaken identity. Their attorneys have provided evidence to support their claims, although police and the FBI have not yet commented on the emails.
